steps.text: We start with two linear systems that hardly differ. Only the right-hand side differs in the last digit:
steps.explanation:
On the left the solution is \(x = (1, 1)\). Check: \(1 + 1 = 2\) ✓, \(1 + 1.0001 = 2.0001\) ✓

On the right the solution is \(x = (0, 2)\). Check: \(0 + 2 = 2\) ✓, \(0 + 2.0002 = 2.0002\) ✓

The right-hand side changed by \(0.0001\) – that is about \(0.005\,\%\). The solution, however, changed completely: from \((1, 1)\) to \((0, 2)\), i.e. by \(100\,\%\)!

No arithmetic mistake, no rounding error – this is exact mathematics.
steps.section: Chapter 1 · An uncanny linear system
steps.insight: Some linear systems react extremely sensitively to tiny changes in the data.

steps.text: Geometrically, each equation is a line and the solution is their intersection. Here the two lines are almost parallel:
steps.explanation:
The slopes of the two lines \(x_2 = 2 - x_1\) and \(x_2 = \frac{2.0001 - x_1}{1.0001}\) hardly differ. Shift one line by a tiny amount and the intersection moves far along the lines. (For visibility, the animation shows a slightly less extreme version with \(1.1\) instead of \(1.0001\) – the effect is the same.)

This is exactly the ill-conditioning from the lesson “Conditioning & Stability” – now for linear systems. To measure it we need two tools:
1. Norms: how large is a vector? (for relative errors of \(x\) and \(b\))
2. Matrix norms: how strongly can a matrix stretch vectors?

With these we finally define the condition number \(\operatorname{cond}(A)\) – and compute it for this example.
steps.section: Chapter 1 · An uncanny linear system
steps.insight: Almost parallel lines = ill-conditioned linear system. Goal of this lesson: express that in one number.

steps.text: For numbers the relative error is \(\frac{|\tilde{x} - x|}{|x|}\). For vectors we need a replacement for the absolute value \(|\cdot|\). The best-known option is the length:
steps.explanation:
This is Pythagoras' theorem, the Euclidean norm (2-norm).

Example: \(x = (3, 4)\): \(\|x\|_2 = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5\).

The double bars \(\|\cdot\|\) distinguish the norm from the absolute value of a number.
steps.section: Chapter 2 · How large is a vector? Norms
steps.insight: A norm measures the “size” of a vector. The 2-norm is the ordinary length.

steps.text: But there are other sensible ways to measure the size of a vector. Two of them are especially popular in numerical analysis:
steps.explanation:
For \(x = (3, 4)\):
• \(\|x\|_1 = 3 + 4 = 7\): the distance a taxi has to drive in a city with a rectangular street grid (hence “Manhattan norm”).
• \(\|x\|_\infty = \max(3, 4) = 4\): the component of largest magnitude (“maximum norm”).

Why several norms? The 1-norm and the \(\infty\)-norm are much easier to compute (no square root), and the \(\infty\)-norm answers a practical question: how large is the error in the worst component?
steps.section: Chapter 2 · How large is a vector? Norms
steps.insight: 1-norm: sum of magnitudes. \(\infty\)-norm: largest magnitude. 2-norm: length.

steps.text: An example with three components: \(x = (1, -2, 2)\).
steps.explanation:
Careful with the absolute values: the \(-2\) counts as \(2\), not as \(-2\).

The three norms give different numbers – but all describe how large \(x\) is. Notice: \(\|x\|_\infty \le \|x\|_2 \le \|x\|_1\). This always holds, as we will see shortly.
steps.section: Chapter 2 · How large is a vector? Norms
steps.insight: Different norms, different numbers – but always the same order of magnitude.

steps.text: What makes a function a norm? Three properties that any reasonable “size” should have:
steps.explanation:
In words:
1. Only the zero vector has size zero.
2. A vector twice as long is twice as large – reversing the direction changes nothing.
3. A detour is never shorter than the direct route.

All three norms \(\|\cdot\|_1\), \(\|\cdot\|_2\), \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\) satisfy these rules.
steps.section: Chapter 2 · How large is a vector? Norms
steps.insight: Norm = positivity + scaling + triangle inequality.

steps.text: A nice picture of the differences: draw all vectors with norm \(1\), the so-called unit circle of each norm.
steps.explanation:
• 2-norm: the familiar circle.
• 1-norm: a rhombus (a square standing on its tip), because \(|x_1| + |x_2| = 1\) consists of four straight pieces.
• \(\infty\)-norm: a square, because \(\max(|x_1|, |x_2|) = 1\) means: one component is \(\pm 1\), the other at most that large.

The rhombus lies inside, the square outside, the circle in between. This matches the order \(\|x\|_\infty \le \|x\|_2 \le \|x\|_1\): whoever is small in the 1-norm is all the more small in the others.
steps.section: Chapter 2 · How large is a vector? Norms
steps.insight: Unit circles: rhombus (1-norm), circle (2-norm), square (\(\infty\)-norm).

steps.text: The norms can be bounded against each other. For \(x \in \mathbb{R}^n\):
steps.explanation:
Check with \(x = (1, -2, 2)\), \(n = 3\): \(2 \le 3 \le 5 \le 3 \cdot 2 = 6\) ✓

Why does the last inequality hold? Each of the \(n\) components has magnitude at most \(\|x\|_\infty\), so together at most \(n \cdot \|x\|_\infty\).

The consequence is called norm equivalence: if a vector is small in one norm, it is small in every other norm too (up to a fixed factor). For convergence and error statements you may therefore choose the most convenient norm.
steps.section: Chapter 2 · How large is a vector? Norms
steps.insight: In \(\mathbb{R}^n\) all norms are equivalent: they differ at most by a factor that depends only on \(n\).

steps.text: Now we can measure relative errors of vectors:
steps.explanation:
Our example from the beginning in the \(\infty\)-norm:
• Solution: \(x = (1, 1)\), perturbed solution \(\tilde{x} = (0, 2)\)
• \(\tilde{x} - x = (-1, 1)\), so \(\|\tilde{x} - x\|_\infty = 1\)
• \(\|x\|_\infty = 1\)
• Relative error: \(\frac{1}{1} = 100\,\%\)

And for the right-hand sides \(b = (2, 2.0001)\), \(\tilde{b} = (2, 2.0002)\):
\(\frac{\|\tilde{b} - b\|_\infty}{\|b\|_\infty} = \frac{0.0001}{2.0001} \approx 5 \cdot 10^{-5}\)

So the amplification factor is about \(\frac{1}{5 \cdot 10^{-5}} = 20\,000\).
steps.section: Chapter 2 · How large is a vector? Norms
steps.insight: Relative error of a vector: norm of the deviation divided by the norm of the vector.

steps.text: Quick check: compute all three norms of \(x = (-3, 0, 4)\).
steps.section: Chapter 2 · How large is a vector? Norms
steps.insight: First take magnitudes, then add (1-norm), square and take the root (2-norm) or take the maximum (\(\infty\)-norm).

steps.text: How “large” is a matrix? A matrix is a map: it takes vectors and makes new ones. The natural question: by what factor can it stretch a vector at most?
steps.explanation:
So you try all vectors \(x\) and see how much longer \(Ax\) is relative to \(x\). The largest stretching factor is the matrix norm.

Because it arises from a vector norm, it is called the induced (or operator) matrix norm. Each of the three vector norms has its own matrix norm: \(\|A\|_1\), \(\|A\|_2\), \(\|A\|_\infty\).
steps.section: Chapter 3 · How large is a matrix?
steps.insight: Matrix norm = largest stretching factor the matrix applies to vectors.

steps.text: A simple example: a diagonal matrix.
steps.explanation:
The matrix stretches the \(x_1\) direction by the factor \(3\) and squeezes the \(x_2\) direction to half.

• Largest stretch: \(3\), for example for \(x = (1, 0)\). So \(\|A\| = 3\) (in all three norms).
• Smallest stretch: \(\frac{1}{2}\), for example for \(x = (0, 1)\).

This smallest stretch will soon become important for conditioning.
steps.section: Chapter 3 · How large is a matrix?
steps.insight: For diagonal matrices the norm is simply the diagonal entry of largest magnitude.

steps.text: Two rules follow from the definition that are needed all the time:
steps.explanation:
The first rule is simply the definition: no vector is stretched by more than \(\|A\|\).

The second follows from it: first \(B\) stretches by at most \(\|B\|\), then \(A\) by at most \(\|A\|\). Together at most \(\|A\| \cdot \|B\|\).

In addition \(\|I\| = 1\) for the identity matrix, because it does not stretch at all.
steps.section: Chapter 3 · How large is a matrix?
steps.insight: \(\|Ax\| \le \|A\|\,\|x\|\) – almost all error estimates are carried out with this inequality.

steps.text: Fortunately you do not have to try all vectors. For the \(\infty\)-norm there is a simple formula – the maximum row sum norm:
steps.explanation:
Example \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\):
• Row 1: \(|1| + |2| = 3\)
• Row 2: \(|3| + |4| = 7\)
• So \(\|A\|_\infty = 7\).

Why? If \(\|x\|_\infty \le 1\), every component of \(x\) has magnitude at most \(1\). The \(i\)-th component of \(Ax\) is then at most the row sum \(\sum_j |a_{ij}|\). The maximum is reached when all \(x_j = \pm 1\) with matching signs: here \(x = (1, 1)\), \(Ax = (3, 7)\) ✓
steps.section: Chapter 3 · How large is a matrix?
steps.insight: \(\|A\|_\infty\): add magnitudes row by row, take the maximum.

steps.text: For the 1-norm it is exactly the other way round – the maximum column sum norm:
steps.explanation:
Same example \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\):
• Column 1: \(|1| + |3| = 4\)
• Column 2: \(|2| + |4| = 6\)
• So \(\|A\|_1 = 6\).

It is reached with \(x = (0, 1)\): \(\|x\|_1 = 1\) and \(Ax = (2, 4)\) with \(\|Ax\|_1 = 6\) ✓

Memory aid: the “1” stands upright like a column, the “\(\infty\)” lies flat like a row.
steps.section: Chapter 3 · How large is a matrix?
steps.insight: \(\|A\|_1\): add magnitudes column by column, take the maximum.

steps.text: The 2-norm is the most beautiful geometrically. The matrix maps the unit circle onto an ellipse – the longest semi-axis is the 2-norm.
steps.explanation:
The animation shows \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\). The unit circle becomes an ellipse with
• longest semi-axis \(3\) in direction \((1, 1)\),
• shortest semi-axis \(1\) in direction \((1, -1)\).

So \(\|A\|_2 = 3\). These are exactly the eigenvalues of \(A\) (\(3\) and \(1\)), because for symmetric matrices:
\(\|A\|_2 = \max |\lambda_i|\).

For general matrices one computes \(\|A\|_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(A^{T}A)}\). The square roots of the eigenvalues of \(A^{T}A\) are called singular values.
steps.section: Chapter 3 · How large is a matrix?
steps.insight: \(\|A\|_2\) = longest semi-axis of the image ellipse. For symmetric matrices: eigenvalue of largest magnitude.

steps.text: An example of a non-symmetric matrix: \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\).
steps.explanation:
Eigenvalues of \(A^{T}A\) from \(\lambda^2 - 30\lambda + 4 = 0\) (trace \(30\), determinant \(200 - 196 = 4\)):
\(\lambda = 15 \pm \sqrt{221} \approx 29.866\) or \(0.134\)

So \(\|A\|_2 = \sqrt{29.866} \approx 5.465\).

Comparison: \(\|A\|_1 = 6\), \(\|A\|_\infty = 7\), \(\|A\|_2 \approx 5.47\). Again the same order of magnitude. Because the 2-norm is more work, by hand one usually computes with the 1- or \(\infty\)-norm.
steps.section: Chapter 3 · How large is a matrix?
steps.insight: The 2-norm needs eigenvalues – the 1- and \(\infty\)-norm only additions. That is why they are popular in exercises and estimates.

steps.text: Quick check: compute \(\|A\|_1\) and \(\|A\|_\infty\) for
steps.explanation:
• Row sums: \(0 + 4 = 4\) and \(1 + 2 = 3\), so \(\|A\|_\infty = 4\).
• Column sums: \(0 + 1 = 1\) and \(4 + 2 = 6\), so \(\|A\|_1 = 6\).

Do not forget the magnitudes: the \(-4\) counts as \(4\).
steps.section: Chapter 3 · How large is a matrix?
steps.insight: Typical mistake: mixing up row and column sums or not taking signs as magnitudes.

steps.text: Now we have all the tools. We solve \(Ax = b\), but instead of \(b\) only a perturbed \(b + \Delta b\) is known. The solution then becomes \(x + \Delta x\) with
steps.formula: A(x + \Delta x) = b + \Delta b \quad \Longrightarrow \quad A\,\Delta x = \Delta b \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \Delta x = A^{-1} \Delta b
steps.explanation:
So the perturbation of the solution is the perturbation of the right-hand side “divided by \(A\)”.

The norm rule gives:
\(\|\Delta x\| \le \|A^{-1}\| \cdot \|\Delta b\|\)

For the relative error we still need a lower bound for \(\|x\|\). From \(b = Ax\) we get \(\|b\| \le \|A\| \cdot \|x\|\), so
\(\frac{1}{\|x\|} \le \frac{\|A\|}{\|b\|}\).
steps.section: Chapter 4 · The condition number of a matrix
steps.insight: Perturbation of the solution: \(\Delta x = A^{-1} \Delta b\). The “larger” \(A^{-1}\), the stronger the effect of the perturbation.

steps.text: Multiplying both inequalities gives the most important estimate of this lesson:
steps.explanation:
The factor \(\operatorname{cond}(A) = \|A\| \cdot \|A^{-1}\|\) is called the condition number of the matrix \(A\). It plays exactly the role of \(\kappa\) from the lesson “Conditioning & Stability”: it says by what factor relative errors can be amplified at most.

Important property: \(\operatorname{cond}(A) \ge 1\), because
\(1 = \|I\| = \|A A^{-1}\| \le \|A\| \cdot \|A^{-1}\|\).

A matrix with \(\operatorname{cond}(A)\) close to \(1\) is called well-conditioned, one with a very large \(\operatorname{cond}(A)\) ill-conditioned.
steps.section: Chapter 4 · The condition number of a matrix
steps.insight: Condition number of a matrix: \(\operatorname{cond}(A) = \|A\| \cdot \|A^{-1}\| \ge 1\).

steps.text: Let's compute the condition number for the example from the beginning (\(\infty\)-norm):
steps.explanation:
The inverse of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix: swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by the determinant. Here \(\det A = 1.0001 - 1 = 0.0001\).

• \(\|A\|_\infty = \max(1 + 1,\ 1 + 1.0001) = 2.0001\)
• \(\|A^{-1}\|_\infty = \max(10001 + 10000,\ 10000 + 10000) = 20001\)
• \(\operatorname{cond}_\infty(A) = 2.0001 \cdot 20001 \approx 40\,004\)

So relative errors in \(b\) can be amplified by the factor \(40\,000\).
steps.section: Chapter 4 · The condition number of a matrix
steps.insight: The tiny determinant makes \(A^{-1}\) huge – and with it the condition number.

steps.text: Does this match our observation? Let's check the estimate:
steps.explanation:
The actual relative error \(1\) (i.e. \(100\,\%\)) is below the bound \(2.0\) ✓

The estimate is an upper bound for the worst case. It can be pessimistic by a certain factor, but it predicts the order of magnitude correctly: a tiny perturbation of \(5 \cdot 10^{-5}\) can produce an error of order \(1\).
steps.section: Chapter 4 · The condition number of a matrix
steps.insight: The perturbation theorem \(\frac{\|\Delta x\|}{\|x\|} \le \operatorname{cond}(A) \frac{\|\Delta b\|}{\|b\|}\) predicts the order of magnitude of the error.

steps.text: For the 2-norm the condition number has a vivid meaning. Remember the image ellipse of the unit circle:
steps.explanation:
\(\|A\|_2\) is the largest stretch, \(\|A^{-1}\|_2\) is the reciprocal of the smallest stretch. So the product is the ratio of largest to smallest stretch.

• \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\): semi-axes \(3\) and \(1\), \(\operatorname{cond}_2 = 3\). Harmless.
• An almost singular matrix turns the circle into a very flat ellipse: in one direction almost everything is “squashed”. That direction can hardly be recovered from \(b\).

For symmetric matrices this is simply \(\frac{|\lambda_{\max}|}{|\lambda_{\min}|}\).
steps.section: Chapter 4 · The condition number of a matrix
steps.insight: \(\operatorname{cond}_2(A)\) measures how strongly \(A\) distorts the unit circle: ratio of the longest to the shortest semi-axis.

steps.text: Some typical condition numbers:
steps.formula:
\begin{array}{l|l}
\text{matrix} & \operatorname{cond} \\ \hline
\text{identity } I & 1 \\
\text{rotation, reflection (orthogonal)} & 1 \ \ (\text{2-norm}) \\
\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} & 3 \ \ (\text{2-norm}) \\
\text{Hilbert matrix } H_3 & 748 \ \ (\infty\text{-norm}) \\
\text{Hilbert matrix } H_{10} & 3.5 \cdot 10^{13} \ \ (\infty\text{-norm})
\end{array}
steps.explanation:
The Hilbert matrix has entries \(h_{ij} = \frac{1}{i + j - 1}\), for example
\(H_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{3} & \frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{1}{3} & \frac{1}{4} & \frac{1}{5} \end{pmatrix}\).
Its rows are very similar – almost linearly dependent. It is the classic example of an ill-conditioned matrix and appears in polynomial least-squares fitting.

Orthogonal matrices are ideal: they do not change lengths, so no error can grow.
steps.section: Chapter 4 · The condition number of a matrix
steps.insight: Orthogonal matrices have the best possible condition number \(1\). Matrices with almost linearly dependent rows are ill-conditioned.

steps.text: A common misconception: “a small determinant means ill-conditioning.” That is not true!
steps.explanation:
The matrix \(0.1 \cdot I\) shrinks every vector uniformly to a tenth. Nothing is distorted, and the inverse \(10 \cdot I\) restores everything perfectly: \(\operatorname{cond} = 0.1 \cdot 10 = 1\).

The determinant is still tiny because it multiplies up with the dimension: \(0.1^{10}\).

Conversely, a matrix with determinant \(1\) can be arbitrarily ill-conditioned, for example \(\begin{pmatrix} 10^{4} & 0 \\ 0 & 10^{-4} \end{pmatrix}\) with \(\operatorname{cond} = 10^{8}\).
steps.section: Chapter 4 · The condition number of a matrix
steps.insight: The determinant is not a measure of conditioning. What matters is \(\operatorname{cond}(A) = \|A\|\,\|A^{-1}\|\).

steps.text: What does the condition number mean for computations on a computer? As for functions, the rule of thumb holds:
steps.explanation:
Gauss with pivoting is backward stable: the computed solution is exact for a system perturbed only on the level of \(u \approx 10^{-16}\). The perturbation theorem then gives:
\(\frac{\|\tilde{x} - x\|}{\|x\|} \lesssim \operatorname{cond}(A) \cdot 10^{-16}\)

Examples:
• \(\operatorname{cond} = 40\,000\) (our example): about 11 to 12 correct digits.
• Hilbert matrix \(H_{10}\), \(\operatorname{cond} \approx 3.5 \cdot 10^{13}\): only about 2 to 3 correct digits – although the algorithm works perfectly!
steps.section: Chapter 4 · The condition number of a matrix
steps.insight: Good method + ill-conditioned matrix = inaccurate result anyway. The conditioning sets the limit.

steps.text: So far only \(b\) was perturbed. In practice the entries of \(A\) are inexact too (measurement, rounding). If \(A\) is perturbed by \(\Delta A\), for small perturbations:
steps.explanation:
It is the same condition number! So it describes the sensitivity to perturbations in \(A\) and in \(b\).

More precisely the bound is \(\frac{\operatorname{cond}(A)}{1 - \operatorname{cond}(A) \frac{\|\Delta A\|}{\|A\|}} \cdot \frac{\|\Delta A\|}{\|A\|}\). The denominator is almost \(1\) as long as the perturbation is small compared with \(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cond}(A)}\). If the perturbation becomes so large that the denominator reaches \(0\), \(A + \Delta A\) might even be singular.

If both \(A\) and \(b\) are perturbed, the contributions add up:
\(\frac{\|\Delta x\|}{\|x\|} \lesssim \operatorname{cond}(A) \left( \frac{\|\Delta A\|}{\|A\|} + \frac{\|\Delta b\|}{\|b\|} \right)\)
steps.section: Chapter 5 · Perturbations in the matrix
steps.insight: \(\operatorname{cond}(A)\) amplifies relative perturbations in \(A\) and in \(b\) alike.

steps.text:
Quick check: a matrix has \(\operatorname{cond}(A) = 10^{8}\).
a) The data come from measurements with \(0.1\,\%\) accuracy. Is the solution usable?
b) The data are exact and the computation is done in double. How accurate is the solution?
steps.explanation:
a) Relative data error \(10^{-3}\), amplified by \(10^{8}\): error up to \(10^{5}\), i.e. \(10\,000\,000\,\%\). The solution is completely worthless – no matter how you compute.

b) Relative error about \(10^{8} \cdot 10^{-16} = 10^{-8}\). About 8 digits are correct – usually enough.

The lesson: whether a condition number is “bad” also depends on how accurate the data are.
steps.section: Chapter 5 · Perturbations in the matrix
steps.insight: Expected error ≈ condition number × accuracy of the data. Inaccurate data tolerate only small condition numbers.

steps.text: How do you check a computed solution \(\tilde{x}\) if you do not know the exact one? You plug it in and compute the residual:
steps.explanation:
If \(r = 0\), \(\tilde{x}\) is exact. If \(r\) is small, \(\tilde{x}\) seems good. But beware!

Example: for our system with \(b = (2, 2.0001)\) we try the wrong solution \(\tilde{x} = (0, 2)\):
\(A\tilde{x} = (0 + 2,\ 0 + 2.0002) = (2, 2.0002)\)
\(r = (2 - 2,\ 2.0001 - 2.0002) = (0, -0.0001)\)

The residual is tiny – but the correct solution is \((1, 1)\). The error is \(100\,\%\)!
steps.section: Chapter 6 · Residual and error
steps.insight: A small residual does not automatically mean a small error.

steps.text: The relation between residual and error again follows from the perturbation theorem. The residual is exactly the perturbation of \(b\) for which \(\tilde{x}\) would be exact: \(A\tilde{x} = b - r\).
steps.explanation:
In the example: \(\frac{\|r\|_\infty}{\|b\|_\infty} = \frac{0.0001}{2.0001} \approx 5 \cdot 10^{-5}\). Times \(\operatorname{cond} \approx 40\,000\) this gives an error bound of about \(2\) – matching the actual error \(1\).

So the residual is a good error indicator when the matrix is well-conditioned. For ill-conditioned matrices it can be deceptive.

In the language of the last lesson: the relative residual is the backward error, the error in \(x\) is the forward error – and between them stands the conditioning.
steps.section: Chapter 6 · Residual and error
steps.insight: Relative error ≤ cond(A) · relative residual. Residual = backward error, error = forward error.

steps.text: The residual can even be used to improve a solution. The method is called iterative refinement:
steps.explanation:
The idea: the error \(e = x - \tilde{x}\) satisfies exactly \(Ae = b - A\tilde{x} = r\). Solving this equation (at least approximately) gives a correction \(d \approx e\).

Because the LU decomposition is already available, each refinement step costs only \(O(n^2)\) – very cheap.

Important: the residual must be computed more accurately than the solution (for example in higher precision), otherwise its information is lost through cancellation.
steps.section: Chapter 6 · Residual and error
steps.insight: Iterative refinement: compute the residual, solve the correction equation with the existing LU decomposition, improve the solution.

steps.text: Look back at what you can do now:
steps.explanation:
1. Vector norms: \(\|x\|_1\) (sum of magnitudes), \(\|x\|_2\) (length), \(\|x\|_\infty\) (largest magnitude). All are equivalent: \(\|x\|_\infty \le \|x\|_2 \le \|x\|_1 \le n\|x\|_\infty\).

2. Matrix norms: \(\|A\| = \max \frac{\|Ax\|}{\|x\|}\) = largest stretching factor. \(\|A\|_1\) = largest column sum, \(\|A\|_\infty\) = largest row sum, \(\|A\|_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(A^T A)}\).

3. Condition number \(\operatorname{cond}(A) = \|A\|\,\|A^{-1}\| \ge 1\). For the 2-norm: ratio of the longest to the shortest semi-axis of the image ellipse.

4. Perturbation theorem: \(\frac{\|\Delta x\|}{\|x\|} \lesssim \operatorname{cond}(A) \left( \frac{\|\Delta A\|}{\|A\|} + \frac{\|\Delta b\|}{\|b\|} \right)\).

5. Rule of thumb: \(\operatorname{cond}(A) \approx 10^{k}\) costs about \(k\) digits. The determinant is not a measure of conditioning.

6. Small residual ≠ small error. Iterative refinement improves solutions cheaply.
steps.section: Chapter 7 · Recap
steps.insight: Key message: the algorithm (Gauss with pivoting) ensures a small backward error – \(\operatorname{cond}(A)\) decides how accurate \(x\) is in the end.

steps.text: What comes next? In the next lesson “Least Squares & QR Decomposition” we solve overdetermined systems – more equations than unknowns, as with series of measurements.
steps.explanation:
There the condition number becomes decisive: the obvious route via the normal equations \(A^{T}Ax = A^{T}b\) squares the condition number, because
\(\operatorname{cond}_2(A^{T}A) = \operatorname{cond}_2(A)^2\).

\(10^{6}\) thus becomes \(10^{12}\). The QR decomposition avoids this – with orthogonal matrices, which have condition number \(1\).
steps.section: Chapter 7 · Recap
steps.insight: Orthogonal matrices (condition number 1) are numerical analysis' favourite tool.
